overview: Seeka Limited is one of New Zealand's two largest kiwifruit post-harvest operators, providing an integrated supply chain service from orchard to market across New Zealand and Australia. The company operates 12 packhouse and coolstore facilities covering all major NZ growing regions, owns and leases orchards, and provides retail and wholesale services through its SeekaFresh division. Seeka supplies predominantly to Zespri, the global single-desk kiwifruit marketer, delivered consecutive record profits in FY2024 and FY2025 (record 47.1 million class 1 trays packed), and has now guided a moderation in FY2026 earnings after a hotter, drier growing season reduced volumes from the FY2025 peak.

business_model.summary: Highly seasonal fee-for-service and integrated produce business with approximately 70-90% of gross profit generated in the first half of the calendar year coinciding with the NZ kiwifruit harvest (March-June). Post-harvest operations earn per-tray packing and coolstorage fees from independent growers. Orcharding generates cost-plus margins or profit shares from short and long-term leased orchards that Seeka manages and harvests. SeekaFresh earns commissions on retail sales, wholesale margins, and value-added product revenues. Australian operations are an integrated grower-handler-retailer. The business has strong operating leverage in both directions: FY2024 saw a 44% volume increase drive a 193% EBITDA improvement, FY2025 volumes grew EBITDA a further 26% to a record $96m, while the FY2026 guidance (NPBT $38-42m vs $47.5m in FY2025) illustrates how a below-record season still moderates earnings materially even without a crisis-level weather event.
business_model.customer_type: B2B: primarily Zespri (kiwifruit export marketer) and independent NZ growers for post-harvest/orcharding. B2B/B2C: SeekaFresh serves large-format NZ retailers, Asian exporters, and runs a wholesale fresh produce market.
business_model.geographic_mix: New Zealand approximately 95% of revenue, Australia approximately 5%. NZ operations span Northland (Kerikeri, Orangewood), Coromandel (Peninsula), Bay of Plenty (Katikati, Aongatete, Work Road, Huka Pak, Oakside, KKP, Transpack, OPAC), and Gisborne. Bay of Plenty provides approximately 85% of Seeka's kiwifruit supply.
business_model.seasonality: Highly seasonal - approximately 70-90% of annual gross profit earned in H1 (January-June). This creates significant working capital requirements during harvest and large period-to-period earnings swings within the year.

main_competitors: EastPack Limited (Te Puke-based co-operative, largest operator ~30% market share)
competitive_position.market_position: Seeka is one of the two largest kiwifruit post-harvest operators in New Zealand alongside EastPack. Seeka packed 47.1 million class 1 trays in 2025 (a record) and 45.4 million in the 2026 season, from a total NZ industry of approximately 215-220 million trays, representing roughly 20-25% market share. Seeka is also the largest single kiwifruit grower (by owned/leased hectares managed) in both New Zealand and Australia. It is the only listed pure-play kiwifruit company on the NZX.

moat_factors.factor: Scale and geographic diversification of infrastructure
moat_factors.description: 12 packhouse facilities across all major NZ growing regions (Northland, Coromandel, Bay of Plenty, Gisborne) plus Australian assets. Capacity exceeding 50 million trays. Scale enables investment in automation (Reemoon technology), data visualisation, and grower management tools unattainable by smaller operators. Regional spread reduces single-event weather risk, though the 2026 season showed a broad hot/dry pattern can still compress volumes across regions simultaneously.

Seeka's orcharding operations grew approximately 40% of the fruit it handled in post-harvest in FY2024-2025. This vertical integration creates a captive volume base that reduces revenue volatility versus post-harvest-only operators and deepens grower relationships. Long-term lease co-investments with iwi (Raukokore) and government agency Kanoa further entrench supply commitments.

Multi-year orchard management contracts, a grower loyalty share scheme, and integrated services create switching costs and loyalty. High pre-season grower sign-up rates (highlighted by management as a key metric). Seeka app provides real-time fruit tracking from NZ packhouse to offshore markets, adding grower value.

KKP automated packing machine, Oakside and Gisborne upgrades, and 2026-season Reemoon installations at Kerikeri and Huka Pak have structurally reduced per-tray costs. Total expenses per tray were down 19% in FY2024 despite 44% volume growth. Management confirmed in the June 2026 guidance that automation investments are helping offset ongoing cost pressures even as volumes eased. Automation creates a competitive advantage in labour cost and throughput management.

Seeka is an accredited Zespri Registered Supplier with BioGro-certified organic packhouses. These accreditations are necessary to participate in the single-desk export programme and signal quality standards to growers. Seeka's track record of low onshore fruit loss and excellent offshore quality is a competitive differentiator for grower retention.

weaknesses: Revenue is fundamentally volume-driven and highly sensitive to weather, creating binary year-to-year earnings outcomes with no natural hedge - illustrated again by the FY2026 guidance downgrade following a hotter, drier season
High fixed-cost base (12 packhouses, coolstores, 650+ permanent staff) amplifies earnings volatility when volumes decline
EastPack and other co-operatives can offer growers equity ownership stakes that Seeka, as a public company, cannot match
Concentrated customer: Zespri as single-desk exporter limits pricing leverage on post-harvest service fees

SeekaFresh and Australian businesses remain subscale contributors relative to total capital employed, and Australia's FY2026 volumes fell 14% on adverse weather, delaying the expected scale-up from new developments

growth_drivers: NZ kiwifruit industry volume growth: Zespri's five-year plan (published January 2026) targets 236 million trays by 2030 (from 214 million in 2025, +10%). Up to 400 hectares of new SunGold licences are being released in 2026 (up from 350ha previously signalled), with a further 350-500ha planned for 2027-2029. Seeka's packhouse capacity (>50m trays) is in place to capture its share of industry growth without major additional capital.

SunGold (Gold3) variety shift: SunGold is the premium higher-margin variety with growing per-hectare yields. The 2026 harvest included record SunGold volume even as total Class 1 trays fell to 45.4m (from 47.1m) because Hayward (Green) volumes normalised lower. Zespri projects SunGold to grow 17% to 163.5m trays by 2030. Continued SunGold mix-shift underpins earnings quality improvement even in a down-volume year.

Post-harvest automation delivering structural cost reduction: Reemoon technology installations at Kerikeri and Huka Pak for the 2026 season, plus evaluation of a 'lights-out' fully automated coolstore, are allowing more fruit to be handled at lower per-unit costs, partially offsetting the volume shortfall and ongoing input cost inflation flagged in the June 2026 guidance.

Orchard development pipeline entering production: 70+ hectares co-developed with iwi in Raukokore (first crop 2025, volumes growing), plus $7.1m invested in 15 ha kiwifruit and 13 ha avocado on long-term leased land. These orchards will progressively increase Seeka's captive volume supply through 2026-2030, though the pace of ramp can be masked in any single hot/dry season.

Australian business scale-up from new developments: $17.2m invested in new Australian orchard developments (64 ha kiwifruit, new pear varieties, jujube expansion, Ruby Roo nashi launch). Expected production growth from these developments did not materialise in the 2026 season due to a hotter and drier than usual growing season (Australian kiwifruit harvest down 14% to 2.25m kg), pushing the anticipated earnings lift into future seasons.

Debt reduction reducing financial drag: Net bank debt fell from $172m (2023) to $137m (2024) to $100.3m (December 2025), a leverage ratio of approximately 1.0x EBITDA. Lower interest costs are flowing through to after-tax returns and further debt reduction improves dividend capacity.

Supplementary packing categories improving asset utilisation: Citrus, persimmon, kiwiberry and avocado packing use packhouse capacity during off-peak kiwifruit periods. Banana ripening and tropical fruit import/conditioning via SeekaFresh add year-round revenue to the fixed-cost base.

Value-added products and diversification: SeekaFresh LUVO oil (avocado, olive, macadamia, coconut, following the 2025 Olivado asset purchase), Kiwi Crush dietary supplement, and wholesale fresh produce market provide modest but growing diversified revenue streams.

business.description: Kiwifruit yields are highly sensitive to growing conditions. Seeka's EBITDA ranged from $26m (FY2023, low volumes from Cyclone Gabrielle and drought) to $96m (FY2025, record volumes), and FY2026 NPBT guidance of $38-42m (down from $47.5m) after a hotter, drier season demonstrates the pattern persists even without a major storm event. The Bay of Plenty provides approximately 85% of Seeka's kiwifruit supply, creating geographic concentration risk. Inadequate winter chill, spring frost, wind damage, heat/drought stress, and cyclones can each materially reduce volumes.

Approximately 60% of Seeka's revenue is generated through the Zespri system. Zespri holds the mandated single-desk export licence under NZ Kiwifruit Export Regulations. Any regulatory change removing or weakening this mandate, changes to Zespri's pool allocation methodology, or shifts in Zespri's service fee expectations would directly impact Seeka. Seeka has limited negotiating leverage with Zespri given its scale advantage.

business.risk: Grower retention and competition for supply
business.description: EastPack and other co-operative operators can offer growers equity ownership that Seeka cannot as a public company. Pre-season grower signup rates are a critical operational metric. Loss of significant grower supply to competitors reduces volumes and increases per-unit fixed costs disproportionately.

Psa-V bacterial canker has been endemic in NZ kiwifruit since 2010 and remains a persistent yield and vine health risk. The SunGold Gold3 variety has better Psa tolerance but is not immune. A new virulent Psa strain or adverse weather creating conditions favourable to Psa proliferation could impact vine productivity across Seeka's growing and post-harvest network. Australian operations are also Psa-affected, with an ongoing crop protection programme.

The high fixed-cost structure (packhouses, coolstores, permanent workforce) means a reduction in volumes creates a disproportionate EBITDA/NPBT decline. The FY2026 guidance cut to $38-42m NPBT from $47.5m in FY2025 (a decline of roughly 12-20%) on only a modest tray reduction (45.4m vs 47.1m, ~4%) illustrates the operating leverage. A return to FY2023-level volumes (~30m trays) would likely produce a pre-tax loss again. This binary earnings profile is the fundamental investment risk in the stock.

financial.description: Net bank debt of $100.3m at December 2025 (down significantly from $172m peak, leverage ~1.0x EBITDA). Banking covenants include a 3.25x net leverage ratio and 2.00x interest cover ratio. Seeka required covenant waivers in mid-2023 following the Cyclone Gabrielle crop losses. A return to poor growing conditions could challenge covenant compliance again, though current headroom is comfortable given the FY2026 guidance still implies a profitable year. Banking facility is a sustainability-linked loan of $201m total.

The seasonal business requires significant working capital to fund harvest operations, packhouse costs, and grower advance programmes in H1 before cash is collected from Zespri later in the season. Peak working capital needs require substantial drawdown of the banking facility in the first half. At June 2025, trade and other receivables were $121.8m with $40.9m in advances to growers outstanding.

The 2024 NZ legislation removing tax deductibility of building depreciation created a $12.5m one-off non-cash deferred tax charge in FY2024 and increased total deferred tax liabilities materially. This creates an ongoing wedge between NPBT and reported NPAT, though the effect normalised in FY2025 (EPS of $0.76 versus normalised $0.51 in FY2024).

Australian operations (~5% of revenue) are conducted in AUD creating translation risk. Some USD exposure exists through Zespri's export pricing. Currency movements are secondary in magnitude to volume and operating risks.

regulatory.description: Seeka employs over 1,200 RSE (Recognised Seasonal Employee) workers from Pacific nations plus approximately 1,200 other seasonal staff. RSE scheme quotas, immigration policy, and Accredited Employer Work Visa conditions directly affect labour availability and cost during the critical harvest window. Labour supply constraints have eased since 2024 but remain policy-dependent and could re-tighten.

Zespri's export monopoly is granted under NZ Kiwifruit Export Regulations and periodically comes under review. Any change to the regulatory framework would restructure the kiwifruit supply chain and could fundamentally alter grower-packhouse commercial relationships.

Seeka is subject to XRB's NZ Climate Standards NZ CS 1-3. Absolute emissions rose materially in high-volume years due to increased throughput and refrigerant use. Increasing emissions intensity during high-volume years creates potential compliance and reputational risks as emissions reporting and carbon pricing frameworks develop. Seeka's 2026 Sustainability Report (released 30 June 2026) details progress including further eco-friendly coolant retrofits (3 coolstores in the FY2025 year).

International market access for NZ kiwifruit depends on phytosanitary standards managed by MPI and Zespri. Any new biosecurity detections, pest incursions, or quality failures could trigger market access restrictions affecting the entire industry supply chain.

macro.risk: Climate change and extreme weather events
macro.description: The 2023 season was severely impacted by Cyclone Gabrielle, and the 2026 season was hit by a hotter and drier than usual growing season in both New Zealand and Australia, reducing volumes and delaying expected production growth from new orchard developments. Climate research indicates that the core Bay of Plenty growing region may face increasing production challenges from changing weather patterns including reduced winter chill, increased drought frequency, and more intense cyclonic events. Seeka is responding with regional diversification and rootstock research but cannot fully mitigate systemic weather risk, and two of the last four seasons (2023, 2026) have now shown material weather-driven earnings shortfalls versus prior guidance or trend.

Zespri achieved record global sales of NZ$5.14b in 2024/25 with 220.9m trays and strong per-tray returns. However, Zespri's global licensing programme has expanded SunGold production in Italy, France and other Northern Hemisphere markets, which will eventually create more supply competition for the NZ-grown premium. Unauthorized Chinese SunGold production also dilutes variety positioning, though Zespri has been winning legal battles against it.

Management continues to flag cost pressures (labour, electricity, packaging) as ongoing challenges, noting in the June 2026 guidance that automation investment is helping offset these pressures. NZ labour costs (minimum wage, RSE scheme rates) continue to rise. Automation is Seeka's primary mitigation.

execution.description: Seeka has committed capital to new Australian orchard developments (kiwifruit, pear, jujube, and the new Ruby Roo nashi variety) intended to lift Australian earnings from 2026. The expected production growth did not materialise in the 2026 season due to adverse weather (harvest down 14% to 2.25m kg), pushing the anticipated scale-up and return on this investment further out. Achieving acceptable returns on invested capital requires successful Psa management, crop quality improvement, and market development in a geography where Seeka lacks its NZ scale advantages.

The Reemoon technology installations at Kerikeri and Huka Pak for the 2026 season represent significant capital commitments. Integration complexity, commissioning downtime during harvest, and the need to optimise technology for each fruit type and quality profile creates execution risk. Management commentary in mid-2026 credits automation with helping offset cost pressures, a positive early signal, but full performance validation typically takes several seasons (as seen with the earlier KKP automated line).

Chair Mark Dewdney (appointed December 2024) and director Hayley Gourley (January 2025) replaced long-serving Ashley Waugh (10 years) and Fred Hutchings (12 years as Chair). Board transition during a period of strategic momentum is manageable given CEO Michael Franks' operational continuity, but the full value of new board relationships and oversight style is still being established, and the board's handling of the first down-guidance year since FY2023 will be a test.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: The NZ kiwifruit industry remains in a structural growth phase even after a softer 2026 season. Zespri's five-year outlook (published January 2026) targets 236 million trays by 2030 (up 10% from 214 million in 2025), with SunGold projected to grow 17% to 163.5m trays and RubyRed more than doubling. Up to 400 hectares of new SunGold licences are being released in 2026 (up from 350ha previously signalled), with 350-500ha planned annually through 2029. The 2026 harvest itself came in below the exceptional 2025 record due to hot, dry conditions, illustrating that near-term season-to-season volume growth is not guaranteed even as the multi-year structural trend remains positive. The key uncertainty is the competitive impact of Northern Hemisphere licensed SunGold production (Italy, France) on per-tray returns over the 5-10 year horizon.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High operational cyclicality within years (H1-heavy with 70-90% of annual gross profit) and significant year-to-year swings driven by harvest volumes. Seeka's EBITDA/NPBT ranged from $26m EBITDA (FY2023) to $96m EBITDA / $47.5m NPBT (FY2025), with FY2026 NPBT guided down to $38-42m. Unlike typical agriculture, however, the industry benefits from Zespri's single-desk coordination which provides some demand-side stability through premium market management even when volumes vary.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate. Net bank debt of $100.3m at December 2025 on a variable-rate sustainability-linked facility means NZ OCR movements directly affect interest expenses. Interest costs have declined materially as both debt levels and rates have fallen since the FY2023 peak, providing a tailwind that partially offsets the FY2026 volume-driven earnings moderation.
key_input_costs: Labour: largest cost driver - approximately 650 permanent staff plus 1,200 RSE seasonal workers and 1,200 other seasonal staff.
Electricity: powers packhouses and coolstores, a major operating expense subject to NZ electricity market pricing. Seeka continues to invest in solar and natural refrigerants to manage this exposure.
Packaging materials: trays, cartons, labels scale directly with volumes. Inflationary pressures noted by management as an ongoing cost challenge, partially offset by automation efficiency gains.
Refrigerants: transitioning to natural refrigerants to reduce both operational costs and emissions; 3 coolstores retrofitted with eco-friendly coolants per the FY2025 annual report.
Fuel: transport fleet for orchard-to-packhouse logistics and outbound distribution.

recent_developments.event: Seeka advised the release date for its half-year 2026 result (period ending 30 June 2026). As of 1 August 2026 the H1-2026 result itself had not yet been published; based on prior-year pattern (20 August 2025 release) it is expected in mid-to-late August 2026.
Seeka released its 2026 Sustainability Report, detailing progress on emissions reduction, coolant retrofits, and other ESG initiatives under NZ Climate Standards reporting obligations.

Seeka provided its first earnings guidance for 2026, alongside confirmation of a completed 2026 kiwifruit harvest. NPBT guided to $38.0m-$42.0m, down from $47.5m in FY2025 but still the company's second-highest result on record. NZ Class 1 tray volumes were 45.4 million (down from the record 47.1 million in 2025), with record SunGold volume offset by lower, more normal Hayward (Green) yields. Australian kiwifruit harvest fell 14% to 2.25 million kg due to a hotter and drier than usual growing season, meaning expected production growth from new Australian orchard developments did not materialise in 2026. Management noted cost pressures remain but automation investments are helping offset them, and flagged the guidance as preliminary subject to update if material changes occur.

FY2025 annual result released (year ended 31 December 2025): Revenue $439.6m/$440m (+7% on FY2024's $411.4m), EBITDA $95.9m/$96m (+26%), EBIT $62.6m (+34%), NPBT $47.5m (+60%), NPAT $32.0m (+265% reported, +50% on FY2024 normalised $21.2m), EPS $0.76 (vs normalised $0.51 in FY2024, +49%). Gross profit $125.9m (+20%) at 28.6% margin. Total assets $605.4m (+10%), total equity $298.1m. Operating cash flow $79.0m (+20%). Net bank debt $100.3m, down 27% from $137.3m. Post-harvest packed record 47.1m class 1 trays (+10%); SunGold 28.7m trays (+9%). Orcharding grew 19.0m trays (+10%). Board acknowledged it was 'too early to reliably indicate 2026' but noted positive early winter chill indicators (which the subsequent June 2026 guidance showed did not fully translate into a repeat record season due to a hot, dry spring/summer).

Seeka announced a fully imputed dividend of 25 cents per share, paid 15 April 2026 (record date 20 March 2026), with the DRP applying at a 2% discount to VWAP. This brought total capital returned to shareholders across FY2025 payments and the declared April 2026 payment to $0.55/share over roughly 12 months.

H1-2025 interim results: Revenue $307.9m (+8%), EBITDA $83.5m (+22%), NPBT $59.4m (+32%), NPAT $37.8m (+121%). Packed 47.1m class 1 trays (+10% vs H1-2024's 43.0m). Net bank debt $130.6m (down $40.2m YoY). Full year NPBT guidance raised to $35-39m (from $33-37m), later beaten with actual FY2025 NPBT of $47.5m. Declared $0.15/share dividend for October 2025.

Seeka purchased the assets of Olivado, resetting SeekaFresh's avocado oil manufacturing and marketing business (now branded LUVO oil, encompassing avocado, olive, macadamia and coconut oils). Provides local capacity to process oil-grade avocado in Northland and adds integrated processing capability to the SeekaFresh segment.

Ruby Roo (new red nashi variety developed by Plant and Food Research/Prevar) launched into the Australian market, grown on Seeka's Australian orchards, diversifying the Australian product portfolio beyond kiwifruit and traditional nashi.

Zespri published its updated Five-Year Outlook targeting 236 million trays by 2030 from 214 million in 2025 (10% growth). SunGold projected to grow 17% to 163.5m trays; RubyRed to more than double. Up to 400 hectares of new SunGold licences to be released in 2026 (up from 350ha previously signalled), with 350-500ha planned annually 2027-2029. These industry volume targets underpin Seeka's long-term packhouse utilisation outlook even though the near-term 2026 season came in below the 2025 record.

items.vs_prior: lowered vs FY2025 actual of $47.5m (would be the second-highest NPBT on record if achieved)
items.notes: First formal FY2026 guidance, issued 17 June 2026 alongside confirmation the 2026 harvest was complete. Reflects a hotter and drier than usual growing season that reduced NZ Class 1 tray volumes and Australian kiwifruit harvest weight versus the FY2025 record. Management flagged the guidance as preliminary and subject to update for material changes.

items.vs_prior: down from the record 47.1 million trays in 2025 (~-4%)
items.notes: Record SunGold volume was offset by lower, more 'normal' Hayward (Green) yields versus the exceptional 2025 season.
Hotter, drier growing season delivered a smaller fruit size profile and lower earnings; expected production growth from new Australian orchard developments did not materialise in 2026.
Management noted cost pressures remain significant but that recent automation investments (Reemoon at Kerikeri and Huka Pak) are helping offset these expenses.

items.vs_prior: record results, beat interim guidance range of $35-39m NPBT by a wide margin
items.notes: Basis of comparison for the FY2026 guidance reduction.

Leverage ratio approximately 1.0x EBITDA. No updated net debt figure disclosed with the June 2026 guidance; H1-2026 result (release date advised 27 July 2026, not yet published as of 1 August 2026) will provide the next formal update.

items.vs_prior: part of $0.55/share total returned to shareholders over the preceding ~12 months ($0.10 Jan-25, $0.05 Apr-25, $0.15 Oct-25, $0.25 Apr-26)
items.notes: No new dividend guidance issued alongside the June 2026 NPBT guidance; next dividend decision expected with the H1-2026 result.

guidance.management_commentary: Management's June 2026 guidance described the season as delivering the company's second-highest NPBT on record despite the shortfall versus FY2025, framing the moderation as a return to more typical conditions after an exceptional prior year rather than a structural deterioration. The commentary reiterated that Seeka operates a highly seasonal business with the majority of profit generated in H1, and that cost pressures are being partly offset by automation investment. Guidance was explicitly flagged as preliminary and subject to update should material changes occur before the H1-2026 result (release date advised late July 2026, result not yet published as of 1 August 2026).

bull_case: FY2026 guidance of $38-42m NPBT would still be the second-highest result in company history, indicating the FY2024-25 earnings recovery reflects genuine structural improvement (automation, debt reduction, normalised labour supply) rather than a one-off weather-driven spike that fully reverses in a softer year.

Powerful industry tailwinds with Seeka's capacity already in place: Zespri's five-year plan targets 10% industry volume growth to 236m trays by 2030, led by SunGold expansion (+17% to 163.5m trays) and up to 400ha of new SunGold licences released in 2026 alone. Seeka has >50m tray post-harvest capacity in place without requiring major capital expenditure, so continued industry growth flows through at high incremental margins.

Automation investment cycle creating durable cost advantage: Reemoon technology at Kerikeri and Huka Pak, credited by management with helping offset cost pressures even in the softer 2026 season, reduces per-tray costs and dependence on the RSE labour programme. A potential future 'lights-out' automated coolstore could be transformative for coolstore asset returns.

Balance sheet materially de-risked: net bank debt down from $172m (2023 peak) to $100.3m (December 2025), leverage around 1.0x EBITDA, giving Seeka headroom to absorb a down-guidance year like FY2026 without covenant stress and to keep funding the orchard development and automation pipeline.

Dividend resumption signals sustainable profitability: Seeka returned $0.55/share to shareholders over the roughly 12 months to April 2026 after two years without dividends. Even at the lower end of FY2026 guidance the company remains solidly profitable, supporting continuation of capital returns.
bear_case: The June 2026 guidance cut (NPBT to $38-42m from $47.5m) shows the earnings base is still highly volume-sensitive even absent a major cyclone-scale event - a routine hot, dry season was enough to knock 12-20% off NPBT, and the same dynamic hit both New Zealand and Australia simultaneously, undermining the diversification thesis.

Fundamental Zespri concentration and single-desk risk: approximately 60% of Seeka's revenue flows through the Zespri system. Seeka cannot independently market kiwifruit internationally and has limited pricing power on post-harvest service fees. Any regulatory change to the single-desk structure or deterioration in Zespri's global market performance would directly harm Seeka with no alternative outlets.

Australian expansion returns delayed again: expected production growth from new Australian orchard developments (kiwifruit, pear, jujube, Ruby Roo nashi) did not materialise in 2026 due to adverse weather, with the harvest down 14%. This is the second consecutive period in which Australian scale-up has underdelivered against plan, raising questions about the payback timeline on this capital.

Valuation risk after a two-year earnings recovery: the historical earnings range is extremely wide - from a $21m pre-tax loss in FY2023 to $47.5m NPBT in FY2025 - and the stock may still be priced off the record FY2025 base rather than the now-guided FY2026 moderation. A further poor season (repeat of FY2023-level conditions) would again test covenant headroom and dividend sustainability.

Northern Hemisphere SunGold competition emerging: Zespri's global licensing programme has expanded SunGold production across Italy, France and other Northern Hemisphere growers. While currently complementary to NZ supply (different seasons), increasing licensed Northern Hemisphere volumes will eventually put pressure on the price premium earned for NZ-grown SunGold as total global supply rises faster than demand.
